Case study · Prime League · 2023

An esports platform people can follow

Prime League ran several leagues on one platform, and every path started with the league's data model. As the UX designer on the team, I researched why people got lost and restructured the platform around the one question everyone had: when and where is the next match?

  • −30 % registration drop-off measured
  • +10 % active users measured
  • 50,000+ users per season
Role
UX Designer: research, analysis, ideation and wireframes. The UI came from the team's UI designer.
Team
1 UI designer, 1 product manager, 3 developers
Product
Prime League, 99Damage League and DreamHack Leipzig on one platform, 8 competitions
Method
Hotjar, Maze, moderated usability tests, card sorting with 25 people

Context

Players, teams and spectators couldn't find what they came for

Prime League is one of the largest League of Legends competitions in the DACH region, with 1,500+ teams and 6,000+ registered players per season. The same platform also ran 99Damage League and DreamHack Leipzig. Three groups use it, each with its own question.

  1. Players Compete "When and where is my next match?"
  2. Teams Prepare "Who do we play next, and how strong are they?"
  3. Spectators Watch "Where does the tournament stand right now?"

The platform answered none of them directly. Every path started with the league, then the season, then the division, and the match came last.

What made it hard

Every change had to work for all eight competitions

One navigation served Prime League, 99Damage League and DreamHack Leipzig at once. I was the newest designer on the team and the UI came from the team's UI designer, so my lever was the structure and the research behind it.

What we saw. Hotjar recordings showed people scrolling past the main navigation. In moderated tests they knew roughly where to look, but could not predict what they would find there.

What confirmed it. In a card sort with 25 players, teams and spectators, people grouped content by what they wanted to do around a match.

Insight

The league structure is how the data is stored, not how people use it. The navigation had to start from the match.

The decisions

Rebuilt the structure around the match

Hypothesis. If the navigation starts from the match instead of the league, more people finish registration and come back.

From league-first to match-first navigation

I restructured the information architecture of all 8 competitions around three entry points: compete, prepare, watch. Your next match, your team and the live tournament are now one step from the start page.

From one generic user to three entry points

One generic user would have fit none of the three groups. So players, teams and spectators each got their own way in, built around their own question.

From the league as the front door to the league as a filter

League, season and division stayed, but as filters on the match, team and tournament pages. People who think in leagues can still narrow things down, everyone else starts from the match.

Result

Fewer people dropped out of registration

After the relaunch, registration drop-off fell by 30 % and active users grew by 10 % (measured, Google Analytics). We attribute most of it to taking part in the league getting easier.

What I learned. The Hotjar recordings showed the problem before any interview did.

What I would do differently

Agree on targets before the work starts. We tracked the right numbers in Google Analytics, but shared targets up front would have helped me argue for decisions, especially as the newest designer on the team.

Happy to tell you how the card sort changed the navigation.
